title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 6: Questions on the MOA-AD Decision
keywords: watch the parliamentary Con-ass zoom off
Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's October 26, 2008 Inquirer column answering three questions about the Supreme Court's MOA-AD decision (on the Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front), whose core holding was that negotiators must follow their mandates and that peace agreements must conform to the Constitution and laws

First, that negotiators -- being 'mere agents of the President' -- 'cannot have more powers than their principal,' so while they may 'think outside the box' and even propose Charter changes, 'they cannot act outside of it,' the Constitution being 'the bedrock of the rule of law'

Second, that striking down the MOA-AD did not violate the Bangsamoro right to self-determination, which the Court (citing the Canadian Supreme Court) held is 'fulfilled through internal self-determination' within an existing state and excludes secession absent colonial rule or foreign domination

Third, an explanation of the split votes (8-7 on the procedural mootness issue, 12-3 on the substantive unconstitutionality issue) and how the 'winning party' is determined -- plus a Charter-change 'Update' on the 'separately or jointly' voting question and the Nograles foreign-ownership resolution
sub_topics: The occasion: CJP's prior column on the MOA-AD ruling 'drew piercing questions, many of them from diplomats' (like Austrian lawyer Ambassador Herbert Jager), three of which he answers -- the Court having essentially held that negotiators must 'strictly follow their mandates' and that peace pacts must 'conform to our Constitution and laws'

Q1 -- creativity vs. the Charter: negotiators are 'mere agents of the President' who 'cannot have more powers than their principal'; the country 'is governed by the rule of law, not by the whim or caprice of any person,' whose 'bedrock' is the Constitution, amendable 'only by observing the processes... embedded in the Constitution itself' -- so negotiators may discuss and even propose changes but 'cannot act outside of [the box] on their own'

The MNLF contrast: Chief Justice Puno's concurrence stressed that the 1996 Peace Agreement with the Moro National Liberation Front (not the MILF) succeeded 'because it respected the metes and bounds of the Constitution,' affirming sovereignty and territorial integrity

International stakes: agreements 'have international consequences that could be enforced by international tribunals,' and since national law does not bind international bodies, negotiators 'should be extra careful' lest they 'defile their mandates and become traitors to the very cause they are supposed to espouse'

Q2 -- self-determination: the right (a 'generally accepted principle of international law' adopted as 'part of the law of the land') is 'fulfilled through internal self-determination' -- development 'within the framework of an existing state' -- and 'excludes secession' while respecting 'the territorial integrity of existing states'

The colonial-rule limit: citing the Canadian Supreme Court, external self-determination (political independence) 'arises only when the people are under colonial rule or subjected to foreign domination'; since the Bangsamoros are 'not colonials' and are 'adequately represented' in government, striking the MOA-AD did not violate their right

Q3 -- the vote: there were two issues -- the 'procedural' mootness issue (voted 8-7) and the 'substantive' unconstitutionality issue (divided 12-3) -- with the 'legalistic' way to find the winning party being to count the justices who 'granted' or 'dismissed (or denied)' the petitions in the dispositive portion ('Wherefore')

The Charter-change Update: the Court dismissed 'for being premature' Rep. Adam Relson Jala's petition against House Resolution 730 (a constituent assembly); 28 Cha-cha proposals were pending, and Speaker Nograles's resolution lifting the 40-percent foreign-ownership limit reportedly had 160-plus signatures -- so with 261 legislators (238 reps, 23 senators), three-fourths being 196, a 'joint' vote of 196 signatures could trigger a test case on whether the houses vote 'separately or jointly,' after which 'watch the parliamentary Con-ass zoom off'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's October 26, 2008 Inquirer column, answers three questions -- many raised by diplomats like Austrian lawyer Ambassador Herbert Jager -- about the Supreme Court's MOA-AD decision, whose core holding was that negotiators must follow their mandates and that peace agreements must conform to the Constitution and laws. First, asked whether negotiations can take up matters needing Charter changes or 'think outside the box,' CJP answers that negotiators 'are mere agents of the President' who 'cannot have more powers than their principal'; the country 'is governed by the rule of law,' whose 'bedrock' is the Constitution, amendable only through its own processes -- so negotiators may discuss and propose changes but 'cannot act outside of it,' a point Puno's concurrence underscored by contrasting the 1996 MNLF Peace Agreement (which 'respected the metes and bounds of the Constitution') and warning that careless accords with 'international consequences' can make negotiators 'traitors to the very cause they... espouse.' Second, asked whether striking the MOA-AD violated the Bangsamoro right to self-determination, he explains that the Court held the right 'fulfilled through internal self-determination' within an existing state, excluding secession; citing the Canadian Supreme Court, external self-determination 'arises only when the people are under colonial rule or subjected to foreign domination,' which does not fit the adequately represented Bangsamoros. Third, asked whether the vote was '8-7 or 12-3,' he clarifies that there were two issues -- the procedural mootness issue (8-7) and the substantive unconstitutionality issue (12-3) -- with the winning party found by counting who 'granted' or 'dismissed' the petitions. He closes with a Charter-change 'Update': the Court dismissed Rep. Adam Relson Jala's petition against House Resolution 730 'for being premature,' and with 28 Cha-cha proposals pending and Speaker Nograles's foreign-ownership resolution reportedly nearing 196 of 261 legislators' signatures, he predicts a test case on whether the houses vote 'separately or jointly' -- after which 'watch the parliamentary Con-ass zoom off.'
